messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arthur was a man accustomed to control. As a film director for over two decades, his job was to command chaos—to orchestrate light, sound, and performance into a coherent vision. That sense of command shattered six months ago during a night shoot in a repurposed industrial warehouse. He remembers it not as a story, but as a sequence of stark, silent images: the slow buckle of a steel support beam under the lighting rig, the cloud of dust blooming towards the ceiling, the look of surprise on his cinematographer’s face just before the world went black. He can’t seem to put the sequence into words, but the pictures are perfectly, terribly clear. The crushing weight and the sudden, absolute darkness were followed by a sound he can never forget—the deafening shriek of twisting metal.

These flashes of memory, vivid and intrusive, are not just frightening; for Arthur, they have become evidence of his own failure. He sees the image of himself, frozen for a split second before the collapse, and has come to believe he is fundamentally inadequate, a leader who failed to protect his crew. The clarity of these visual fragments serves as a constant reminder of his perceived helplessness, cementing a deep conviction that his reactions prove he is a lousy coper. This belief that he is no longer the capable man he once was makes the world feel impossibly dangerous. If he couldn't handle that moment, he feels certain he cannot handle the future, a fear that keeps his body in a constant state of high alert, scanning every room and bracing for the next catastrophe. His nervous system now seems wired directly to the memory; any sudden, loud sound doesn’t just startle him, it brings the image of falling steel rushing back, his heart pounding as if it’s happening all over again.

This pervasive sense of threat has made his own work environment, once a place of creation, a minefield of triggers. The sudden shout of "Action!", the controlled bang of a prop gun, the deep shadows of a soundstage—all send a jolt of panic through him. To manage this relentless, exhausting state of being superalert, Arthur has begun to fundamentally alter how he lives and works. He avoids circumstances that remind him of the event, most notably darkness. He insists on keeping lights on in every room of the house he shares with his partner and has started turning down projects that require extensive night shoots or location work in dark, enclosed spaces. This retreat is fueled by the shame of who he has become; he feels like an imposter, a man unrecognisable to himself, and his avoidance is a way to hide this new, fragile identity from his colleagues and from himself.

This strategy of avoidance, however, has only tightened the trap. By refusing to enter dark screening rooms or work on loud sets, the memories of the accident have remained frozen and unprocessed. The darkness he so carefully avoids has become inextricably linked with the crushing weight of the collapsed rig, making the visual fragments even more potent and terrifying when they inevitably break through. Each time he makes an excuse to his agent or cancels a meeting, the belief that he is a "lousy coper" intensifies. His shrinking world is, to him, daily proof that the competent, confident director is gone. He also finds himself lost in thought, trying to make sense of it all, constantly asking himself why the event happened to him, a question with no satisfying answer. When this mental churning becomes too much, he distracts himself for hours with old films, a temporary reprieve that only makes the ambient sounds of the city—a car backfiring, a distant siren—feel more jarring and threatening when they finally cut through the quiet.

Arthur finally sought therapy after a humiliating experience last week. During a pre-production meeting in a state-of-the-art screening room, his sound designer, wanting to demonstrate an effect, played a loud, metallic crash in the pitch-dark theatre. Arthur didn't just jump; he cried out and scrambled for the exit, leaving his bewildered team behind. The incident solidified his greatest fear: that he is no longer capable of doing the one thing that has defined his entire adult life. He came to the first session not just to stop being afraid, but with a desperate hope of finding the person he was before the lights went out.
